description: We are a group of enthusiasts looking to make a world a better place
summary:
We built the NASA Earth Information Jukebox, a website that lets people hear ocean currents. It takes NASA’s ECCO2 visualization of global surface currents and turns the motion in it into sound. We measured how the water moves across the whole video: how much it swirls (curl), how much it spreads apart or squeezes together (divergence), and how fast it flows. Each measurement drives its own layer of water sound over a background music track. Swirling water gurgles, spreading water flows, and fast currents rush and roar. Hover over any spot on the video to hear the currents there, or move away to hear the whole ocean change over the year. A mixer lets you adjust each layer.

Ocean currents carry heat around the planet, but most people only ever see them as charts or animations. Sound gives another way in, including for blind and low-vision visitors. The site supports screen readers and keyboard navigation and has adjustable text size and contrast. Anyone who can listen can get a feel for how lively and uneven the ocean is.
details:
The NASA Earth Information Jukebox turns NASA’s ECCO2 visualization of global ocean surface currents into a soundscape you can explore. Press play and you hear the whole ocean. Hover over any spot on the video and the sound changes to match the currents there.

Behind it is a data pipeline. We used optical flow on the video to estimate how the water moves in each frame. From that motion we calculated three things: curl (how much the water swirls), divergence (how much it spreads apart or squeezes together) and magnitude (how fast it flows). We split the map into a 48 by 85 grid. Every half second, we ran a Fourier transform over a two-second window to see how strongly and how quickly each patch of ocean changes. Those results are packed into a small data file the website reads.

In the browser, each measurement controls its own sound layer. Swirling water drives a gurgling layer, which shifts from slow, deep bubbles to quick, bright ones as the swirling speeds up. Spreading and converging water drives a flowing-water layer in the same way. Current speed drives a turbulence layer that goes from a distant rumble to a roar. All of this plays over a music track our team made, which quietens over fast currents so the water comes through. A mixer lets listeners set the balance themselves.

Benefits and intended impact

Ocean currents move heat around the planet, but most people only see them as charts or animations. Sound gives another way in, and it’s one that blind and low-vision visitors can use too. We want people to get an intuitive feel for how uneven and alive the ocean is: calm in some places and turbulent in others, and always changing.

Tools and technologies

  • Data processing: Python with NumPy, SciPy, PyDub, OpenCV and Matplotlib, in Jupyter notebooks (optical flow, curl and divergence, Fourier transforms)
  • Website: JavaScript with React and Vite, styled with CSS
  • Sound: the Web Audio API, used to mix looping recordings live in the browser; FFmpeg to prepare the audio files
  • Data: the ECCO2 ocean model visualization from NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio

What makes it creative

Most sonification projects turn data into musical notes. We used real water sounds, so swirling water actually sounds like swirling water. That makes the link between the data and what you hear easier to grasp. The site works at two scales, too. You can listen to a single eddy, or step back and hear the whole ocean change across the year.

What our team considered

  • Accessibility: the site supports screen readers and keyboard navigation, with adjustable text size, a light or dark theme and visible keyboard focus. Explanations sit behind small info icons that open on hover, keyboard focus or tap.
  • Comfort: we kept the water layers quiet by default and made the sound change smoothly, so it stays relaxing rather than jarring.
  • Performance: the full data set is compressed into a 2.7 MB file, and our 96 MB surround-sound track was converted to a 2.7 MB stereo file so the site loads quickly.
  • Honesty about the data: our measurements come from the motion in the visualization, not from the model’s raw velocity data. The sound reflects how the currents look and move rather than exact speeds.
  • Credit: NASA imagery and data are credited on the site.
